letters.headline: A coin for the orchard, and nothing for the orchard
paragraphs: I read that the bank has put out an Orchard Silver Coin, and that Chu growers get nothing from its sales. That sounds about right to me. My apples went to the buyer at the gate this autumn at 3.45 som a kilo, and the glut means nobody is asking for more.
If the bank wants to honour orchards, it could start with a cold store. A coin lasts. An apple in a heap behind the house does not, and no dealer in Bazar-i Kalan will take it back at the same price.
I will not be buying silver. But I would like to know how many coins there are and what they cost, as the paper says, before anyone tells my neighbours it is a good gift. Storage first, prices later.
letters.name: Toktosun Abdraev
letters.reply: The Herald has asked the Bank of Irad for the mintage and the issue price and will print the reply when it comes.

letters.headline: Boots are a fine measure of pay
paragraphs: Your editorial on teachers' pay used boots as its example, and I can tell you it is not a figure of speech. In Toktogul every teacher I know has the same winter list: boots, a coat, coal or wood, and something for the children's school bags.

I teach the younger classes. My pay is close to what the Statistics Office says a teacher earns, and I count it in som because that is how it arrives. My father sells his lambs in autumn, also for som, and then buys hay at 26 som a bale for the winter. He says the som still buys hay. It does not buy much that comes from over the line.

I do not know whether indexing to the bazaar rate is the right answer. The paper is right that the changers swing. But a teacher is not asking for a gift, only for someone to say, in writing, what our pay is meant to be worth by spring. A sentence about som is not that.
letters.name: Ainura Asylbek kyzy

letters.headline: Count the codes on my row yourselves
paragraphs: You write that the bazaar codes mostly point to Tulpar. Come to Dastgoh bazarı and walk my row. Of the stalls I can see from mine, a few have a square code taped to the counter and most take only cash. Nobody asked us, and nobody has counted, as you say yourselves.

I do not mind the code. My nephew put it up so the young ones can pay without hunting for change. But the girl at the next stall who takes it says she cannot touch the money until she finds a Tulpar point, and the point is two buses away. A customer's payment that has to be changed back into real money is not much of a payment.

When Tulpar Pay settles only in coins from January, I will keep my cash box and my som. I have been selling here since the Heavy Machine Plant had eleven thousand workers, and I have seen enough new money.
letters.name: Larisa Pokrovskaya

letters.headline: We drive past the billboard every Sunday
paragraphs: My wife and I have saved for a flat for four years, and the billboard on the Trans-Talas Highway for Alma-Bak is the first thing that has made us believe it could happen. Eleven blocks, due in 2027. Then I read your piece and saw that nobody has published a price or even a bank.

We are not rich and we are not lawyers. When Prof. Akmatova says to ask for the land title, the permit for our block and the company's earlier buildings, I believe her, but I would not know where a person like me asks. Do we go to the company, or to the city, or to the Register of Firms?
I would also like to know whether anything has been poured yet. From the road, I see a fence and some cranes. That is all.
letters.name: Nurlan Tilek
letters.reply: Readers can look a firm up in the Register of Firms, which e-Irad's firm check also covers. The company had not answered the Herald's questions by deadline, and we will ask again.
